content: Exercise has a significant impact on reducing glycated hemoglobin (HbA1c) levels, with combined exercise (aerobic and resistance) being more effective than either aerobic or resistance exercise alone. Additionally, exercise improves the ankle-brachial index, which is a measure of peripheral arterial health. However, evidence regarding the relationship between exercise and peripheral neuropathy, as well as the risk of diabetic foot ulcers in individuals with type 2 diabetes mellitus (T2DM), remains insufficient. High-intensity interval training (HIIT) has been shown to significantly improve glycemic control and cardiorespiratory fitness in patients with T2DM compared to moderate-intensity continuous training (MICT) or no training. HIIT also leads to reductions in body mass index (BMI), body fat, fasting insulin, and HbA1c levels, with greater improvements in cardiorespiratory fitness (VO2 peak) than MICT. Resistance exercise (RE) is effective in improving glycemic control in T2DM patients, with high-intensity RE demonstrating greater benefits in reducing HbA1c and insulin levels compared to low-to-moderate intensity RE. This suggests that the intensity of resistance exercise is directly correlated with its effectiveness in managing glycemic parameters. Qigong, a traditional Chinese exercise, has been found to improve blood glucose levels in T2DM patients. However, the quality of evidence is variable, and further high-quality research is needed to confirm its effects and establish its role in diabetes management. Combined exercise training (aerobic and resistance) has been shown to result in more pronounced improvements in HbA1c levels compared to either aerobic or resistance exercise alone. However, the effects on cardiovascular risk factors and weight loss are less consistent, with no significant differences observed among the different exercise modalities in terms of weight loss. Aerobic interval training (INT) has demonstrated significant improvements in cardiorespiratory fitness (VO2 max) and HbA1c levels in T2DM patients compared to MICT or no exercise. However, other cardiometabolic markers and body composition changes were not significantly altered. Despite the limited number of studies, INT appears to be a promising alternative to MICT for improving cardiometabolic health in T2DM patients. Aquatic exercise (AquaEx) has been shown to reduce HbA1c levels after 8–12 weeks of intervention in adults with T2DM. However, there is limited evidence comparing the effects of AquaEx to land-based exercise (LandEx) or no exercise control (Ctrl), and further research is needed to clarify these comparisons. Yoga interventions have been found to improve glycemic control in adults with T2DM. Studies indicate reductions in HbA1c and fasting blood glucose levels, suggesting that yoga may be a beneficial adjunct therapy for diabetes management. However, more rigorous studies are required to confirm these findings and determine the optimal yoga protocols for T2DM patients. Traditional Chinese exercises (TCEs), including Tai Ji Quan, Qigong, and Ba Duan Jin, have been associated with significant reductions in HbA1c and fasting blood glucose levels in T2DM patients. These exercises also show improvements in secondary outcomes such as lipid profiles and blood pressure. However, further studies are needed to better understand the dose-response relationship and duration of exposure required for optimal benefits. Structured exercise intervention programs have been shown to improve insulin resistance in T2DM patients, with moderate evidence supporting their effectiveness. These programs lead to reductions in fasting insulin, HbA1c, and BMI, highlighting their role in managing insulin resistance and glycemic control in T2DM.
